title: Taxable Capital Employed in Canada - SR&ED Glossary
description: Read our Canadian SR&ED glossary to understand Taxable Capital Employed in Canada and how it affects your corporation's R&D expenditure limit.
summary: Taxable capital employed in Canada is the prior-year capital measure that determines a Canadian-controlled private corporation's SR&ED expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable investment tax credit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6 million limit starts decreasing at $15 million of associated-group taxable capital and is eliminated at $75 million.

body.text: Taxable capital employed in Canada is the prior-year capital measure that determines a Canadian-controlled private corporation's SR&ED expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable investment tax credit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6 million limit starts decreasing at $15 million of associated-group taxable capital and is eliminated at $75 million.
Executive Summary and Statutory Architecture of Canadian R&D Incentives

Canada maintains one of the most comprehensive and structurally mature research and development (R&D) tax incentive frameworks in the industrialized world, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. Administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) with legislative policy formulated by the Department of Finance Canada, the SR&ED program operates through a dual-mechanism architecture embedded within the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and the Income Tax Regulations. First, Subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act establishes a dedicated pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, enabling taxpayers to deduct qualifying current and—following landmark legislative restoration effective December 16, 2024—qualifying capital expenditures against income in the current taxation year or carry those unclaimed deductions forward indefinitely to offset future taxable income. Second, Subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act provide an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a specified percentage of the taxpayer's "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year, yielding either a direct reduction of Part I federal tax otherwise payable or, for eligible claimants, a direct cash refund.

The Canadian R&D tax landscape has undergone its most consequential statutory transformation in over a decade following the release of the 2024 Federal Budget consultations, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement on December 16, 2024, and the subsequent enactment of amending legislation in Annual Statutes 2026, c. 3. Historically, legislative amendments enacted in 2012 (Annual Statutes 2012, c. 31) had restricted the SR&ED program by eliminating capital expenditures and lease costs for capital property after December 31, 2013, reducing the basic ITC rate to 15%, and capping arm's-length contract payments at an 80% inclusion rate. Recognizing the necessity of reversing declining business enterprise R&D capital intensity and retaining intellectual property within domestic borders, the federal government committed $600 million over four years starting in 2025–26 (with $150 million per year ongoing) in Budget 2024, followed by comprehensive structural reforms taking effect on December 16, 2024.

These post-December 15, 2024 statutory reforms fundamentally recalibrate the economics of capital-intensive and scaling R&D enterprises across four interconnected legislative dimensions. First, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC has been doubled from $3 million to $6 million. Second, for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) with taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out range for the $6 million expenditure limit has been widened from the legacy $10 million to $50 million corridor to a substantially broader $15 million to $75 million corridor. Third, addressing a long-standing structural disincentive that penalized domestic technology and life-sciences firms upon executing an initial public offering (IPO) on a Canadian stock exchange, the 35% enhanced refundable ITC (up to the $6 million expenditure limit) has been extended to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, subject to a three-year average annual revenue phase-out between $15 million and $75 million, accompanied by an election allowing CCPCs to adopt the same revenue-based calculation. Fourth, effective for depreciable property acquired and available for use on or after December 16, 2024, and lease costs first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024, capital expenditures have been restored to both the Paragraph 37(1)(b) deductible expenditure pool and the Subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure definition, including the reinstatement of Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) rules and 40% refundability on capital ITCs earned within the enhanced expenditure limit.

body.text: Beyond the federal architecture, Canadian corporate taxpayers benefit from a second layer of provincial and territorial R&D tax credits that stack with—and simultaneously reduce—the federal qualified expenditure base as "government assistance" under Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. Provincial regimes exhibit significant structural divergence across jurisdictions, exemplified by Ontario's multi-credit model (comprising the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit, the 3.5% non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit, and the 20% refundable Ontario Business Research Institute Tax Credit), Alberta's incremental Innovation Employment Grant (providing 8% on base expenditures and 20% on incremental spending above a two-year rolling average up to $4 million), and Québec's sweeping 2025–2026 overhaul that replaces five legacy R&D credits with a unified Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization for fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025.
Federal Legislative Framework and Statutory Definitions
The Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

The legal threshold governing whether technical activities qualify for federal and harmonised provincial R&D tax incentives is codified in Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (and formerly mirrored in Section 2900 of Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations). Subsection 248(1) defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statute subdivides qualifying work into three primary research tiers and one bounded category of commensurate support work.

Under Paragraph (a) of the definition in Subsection 248(1), basic research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Such investigations typically occur in laboratory environments, may be published in scientific journals, and seek to uncover fundamental physical, biological, or mathematical phenomena—such as studying a newly discovered virus to better understand its molecular characteristics. Under Paragraph (b), applied research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, such as experimental efforts to develop a vaccine against a newly discovered virus by exploiting specific biochemical characteristics identified during basic research. Under Paragraph (c), experimental development encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. In industrial practice, experimental development represents the overwhelming majority of Canadian SR&ED claims, encompassing activities such as scaling up and optimizing biomanufacturing processes to enable rapid, large-scale vaccine production where scale-up introduces non-trivial technological uncertainties. Finally, under Paragraph (d), support work qualifies where it involves engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided the work is commensurate with the needs—meaning it corresponds in the amount, size, extent, or duration needed to carry out the SR&ED—and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Conversely, Subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes seven enumerated categories of commercial, routine, or non-scientific activity from the definition of SR&ED, even if they occur within a broader corporate innovation lifecycle. Work falling within paragraphs (e) through (k) of the statutory definition—specifically market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection—is statutorily barred and cannot be claimed. However, the CRA draws an essential functional distinction regarding data collection and testing: while routine data collection and routine testing are excluded, data collection or testing carried out specifically to directly support core SR&ED experimental development (such as performing tests on a new experimental vaccine production process during scale-up) qualifies as eligible support work under Paragraph (d). Furthermore, CRA administrative guidelines clarify that activities related to acquiring knowledge or know-how that already exists—such as employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants to apply what they already know, or purchasing proprietary knowledge—do not meet the requirement of attempting to achieve a scientific or technological advancement and are therefore ineligible.

body.text: The CRA "Why" and "How" Eligibility Methodology

In August 2021, the CRA replaced its legacy sector-specific administrative papers and the traditional "Five Questions" presentation with the unified Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives. As confirmed in the CRA's administrative history of the guidelines, both the legacy Five Questions (originally articulated by the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen) and the modern two-requirement framework are derived directly from Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which did not undergo any statutory text change in that consolidation. The guidelines provide a common language for claimants and CRA officials to use when discussing whether work meets the definition of SR&ED in the Act, structuring technical compliance around two mandatory, interdependent pillars: the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement.

The "Why" requirement mandates that the work be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. A technological advancement is not synonymous with business novelty, commercial competitiveness, or product feature complexity. Rather, it requires encountering a technological uncertainty—a systemic limitation, capability gap, or unpredictable interaction within the underlying science or technology that cannot be resolved through standard practice, publicly available knowledge, or routine engineering. Generating new technological knowledge—even when an experiment fails to achieve the desired commercial performance target, provided it advances the technological baseline by demonstrating why a specific hypothesis is invalid—satisfies the "Why" requirement.

The "How" requirement mandates that the work be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The CRA explicitly distinguishes a "systematic investigation or search" from merely having a systematic or organized approach to one's work or utilizing established techniques or professional protocols. To satisfy the "How" requirement, the claimant's technical execution must follow four sequential stages of the scientific method: first, defining a specific scientific or technological problem by establishing the limitations of current knowledge or technology; second, advancing a formal hypothesis towards resolving that problem; third, planning and testing the hypothesis by means of controlled experiment or rigorous mathematical or engineering analysis; and fourth, developing logical conclusions based on the observed results.
Project Grouping Rules on Form T661

A critical operational requirement under the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives is the proper aggregation of eligible activities into an "SR&ED project". An SR&ED project is defined as a set of interrelated activities that together achieve, or attempt to achieve, a specific scientific or technological advancement, and all activities within an SR&ED project must be related to the same advancement. Because businesses organize their internal workflows around commercial deliverables ("business projects") rather than statutory tax definitions, claimants must first separate eligible work from ineligible work (such as marketing the final product) and then group the eligible activities tied to the same underlying advancement into an SR&ED project across one of three CRA-defined structural scenarios.

In the first scenario, where all activities within a single business project are eligible—for example, a business project containing four activities, all of which directly address or support the same advancement—all four activities are grouped together to form one SR&ED project. In the second scenario, where a business project contains a mix of eligible and ineligible work—for instance, a business project containing four activities of which only two are eligible—only the eligible work can form part of the claim, so the claimant strips out the ineligible tasks and groups the two eligible activities to form one SR&ED project. In the third scenario, where eligible work occurs across several distinct business projects—for example, two separate business projects that contain four activities each, where only two activities in each project are eligible—the claimant can group the eligible work across both business projects into a single consolidated SR&ED project, provided that the two eligible activities in each project relate to the exact same scientific or technological advancement. Once the work is grouped into SR&ED projects, the claimant determines the related expenditures for the year; although an SR&ED project may span several years, a claimant may only claim the expenditures incurred during the specific taxation year for which the claim is filed.
Federal Rates, Expenditure Limits, Refundability, and Pool Mechanics
The Section 37(1) Deductible Expenditure Pool

Under Subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada is entitled to deduct in computing income from that business for a taxation year an amount not exceeding the balance in its cumulative SR&ED deductible expenditure pool at the end of the year. The pool operates on an additive, cumulative basis across taxation years. Paragraph 37(1)(a) adds current expenditures on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly by the taxpayer (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i)), payments to eligible subcontractors performing SR&ED on the taxpayer's behalf, and third-party payments to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D corporations (subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) to (iii)). Following the enactment of Annual Statutes 2026, c. 3, Paragraph 37(1)(b) once again adds eligible capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, that is intended for all or substantially all (90% or more) SR&ED use or consumption in Canada.

Against these additions, Paragraph 37(1)(d) mandates a reduction to the pool equal to the total of all amounts of government assistance (such as provincial R&D tax credits and innovation grants) or non-government assistance (as those terms are defined in Subsection 127(9)) in respect of an expenditure described in Paragraph 37(1)(a) or (b) that, at the taxpayer's filing-due date for the year, the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive. Paragraph 37(1)(d.1) further reduces the pool by the total of all amounts each of which is the provincial "super-allowance benefit amount" (within the meaning assigned by Subsection 127(9)). Crucially, federal SR&ED ITCs deducted from tax otherwise payable or refunded in a preceding taxation year reduce the Section 37(1) pool in the subsequent taxation year under Paragraph 37(1)(e), preventing a double benefit while deferring the income inclusion by one fiscal period. Any unutilized balance remaining in the Section 37(1) pool at the end of a taxation year carries forward indefinitely to subsequent taxation years, subject to loss-streaming restrictions upon an acquisition of control under Subsection 37(6.1).
The Subsection 127(9) Qualified Expenditure Pool and ITC Rates

Whereas Section 37 governs income deductions, Section 127 governs the calculation of the federal Investment Tax Credit. At the end of each taxation year, the claimant computes its "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" under Subsection 127(9), which equals the sum of "qualified expenditures" incurred in the taxation year plus qualified expenditures transferred to the claimant by a non-arm's length performer under Subsection 127(13) (reported via Form T1146), less qualified expenditures transferred by the claimant to another party. Unlike the Section 37(1) deductible pool, the Subsection 127(9) SR&ED qualified expenditure pool is an annual amount calculated at the end of each taxation year that does not carry over to another taxation year; instead, it converts immediately into current-year ITCs. Unused non-refundable ITCs generated in a taxation year may be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward up to 20 taxation years (10 years for credits earned in taxation years that ended before 1998) to offset Part I tax otherwise payable under Subsections 127(5) and 127(9).

The statutory rate and refundability of the federal SR&ED ITC depend on the legal classification of the claimant, the nature of the expenditure (current versus capital), and whether the taxation year begins before December 16, 2024, or after December 15, 2024.

body.text: Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: CCPCs vs. ECPCs

The 2024 Fall Economic Statement and Annual Statutes 2026, c. 3 introduced a bifurcated regime for calculating reductions to the $6 million enhanced expenditure limit for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, alongside a harmonisation election. Under the default rule for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations, the expenditure limit is governed by prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $3,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease when the taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and all associated CCPCs) in the immediately preceding taxation year reaches $10,000,000, and becomes nil when the previous year's taxable capital reaches $50,000,000. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit of a CCPC begins to decrease linearly when the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and all CCPCs in an associated group) reaches $15,000,000, becoming nil at $75,000,000. Expressed mathematically for a full 365-day taxation year, the CCPC expenditure limit under the post-December 15, 2024 regime is:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (of the CCPC and all associated corporations) is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000.

Under this linear formula, for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada above $15,000,000, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced by $1 until it is fully extinguished at $75,000,000.

For Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) whose taxation years begin after December 15, 2024, the statute provides access to the 35% enhanced refundable ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures (yielding 100% refundability on current expenditures and 40% refundability on capital expenditures up to the expenditure limit). Because public corporations frequently hold substantial paid-up capital and equity reserves raised on public exchanges that would prematurely disqualify them under a taxable capital test, an ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out based on its average annual revenue over the preceding three fiscal years. Specifically, the ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease when its average annual revenue over the previous three fiscal years exceeds $15,000,000 and becomes nil starting at $75,000,000. Where an ECPC is a member of a consolidated group that prepares consolidated financial statements, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit must be shared among the members of the consolidated group, and the annual revenue reflected in the consolidated financial statements of the group—which present the assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows of the group members as if they were a single economic entity—is used to calculate the average annual revenue and the expenditure limit, even if an entity leaves or joins the group during the year.

Crucially, under Section 3.1.1 of the CRA's Investment Tax Credit Policy, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC or a group of associated CCPCs may elect, under statutory conditions, to calculate its expenditure limit using the exact same three-year average annual revenue method as an ECPC. Where associated CCPCs make this election, the calculation requires aggregating the total of all amounts of average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements for each corporation that is a member of the group for the taxation year in question over the preceding three fiscal years, regardless of whether those corporations were associated during the entirety of that three-year period. This statutory election provides vital structural relief to venture-backed private biotechnology, clean-technology, and deep-technology CCPCs that have raised over $15 million in equity or convertible debt—which inflates their taxable capital employed in Canada—but remain pre-revenue or generate under $15 million in three-year average annual revenue.
Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methods, and Capital Restoration
Detailed Breakdown of Allowable and Qualified SR&ED Expenditures

To claim SR&ED tax incentives on Form T661, a claimant must first determine its allowable SR&ED expenditures and then adjust those figures under Subsection 127(9), Subsection 127(11.5), and Subsection 127(11.6) to arrive at qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes. Before December 16, 2024, the definition of "qualified expenditure" in Subsection 127(9) was restricted to an allowable expenditure of a current nature for SR&ED directly undertaken by the claimant, plus 80% of contract expenditures for SR&ED performed on behalf of the claimant and 80% of third-party payments, plus the prescribed proxy amount. Effective December 16, 2024, the definition of "qualified expenditure" encompasses allowable expenditures of a current nature directly carried out by the claimant, 80% of contract expenditures and third-party payments, the prescribed proxy amount, expenditures for Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, and allowable expenditures of a capital nature acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024.

body.text: Traditional Method vs. Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)

When computing overhead expenditures on Form T661, a claimant must elect annually—an irrevocable election for that taxation year once filed—between two mutually exclusive calculation methodologies: the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA / Proxy Method) and the Traditional Method. Designed to minimize administrative compliance burdens for labour-intensive claimants, the proxy method replaces the granular tracking and substantiation of specific SR&ED overhead expenses with a notional amount equal to 55% of the salary and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (subject to statutory caps for specified employees). Because the PPA is a notional proxy rather than an actual cash expenditure, it is never added to the Section 37(1) pool of deductible expenditures; instead, actual overhead outlays such as utilities, office supplies, and indirect support staff are deducted under ordinary business income rules in Section 9 and Paragraph 18(1)(a), while the PPA is added solely to the Subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool on Form T661 to generate federal (and harmonised provincial) ITCs. Claimants electing the proxy method are expressly prohibited from claiming lease costs for general purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF).

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, the claimant foregoes the notional PPA and instead identifies, substantiates, and claims specific overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 that are directly attributable and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Furthermore, for taxation years with expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, a claimant electing the traditional method may claim the proportionate SR&ED lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% of its operating time on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures, whereas under the proxy method, equipment leased and used less than 90% of the time in SR&ED is deemed captured within the PPA and cannot be claimed separately.
The Restoration of Capital Expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) After December 15, 2024

One of the most technically rigorous compliance areas in modern Canadian R&D tax auditing is the transition regime governing the restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures and lease costs enacted pursuant to the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and Annual Statutes 2026, c. 3. Under the CRA's updated Capital Expenditures Policy and Lease Expenditures Policy, expenditures for depreciable property or for the right to use property acquired after December 31, 2013, and before December 16, 2024, do not qualify for SR&ED tax incentives under any circumstances.

An eligible SR&ED capital expenditure is strictly limited to an expenditure made to acquire new or used depreciable property—defined as property for which Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) can be claimed under Paragraph 20(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act—that is acquired and becomes available for use after December 15, 2024. Because CCA may be claimed only for property owned (or deemed to be owned) by the claimant or property in which the claimant has a leasehold interest, claiming an allowable SR&ED capital expenditure under Paragraph 37(1)(b) requires that the expenditure result in the claimant owning, or obtaining a leasehold interest in, the SR&ED property. A claimant who acquires or holds property merely as an agent or nominee for another party cannot claim the property as an SR&ED capital expenditure, and in computing the income of a partnership under Subsection 96(1) of the Income Tax Act and Subsection 1102(1a) of the Income Tax Regulations, partnership property (including SR&ED property) must be accounted for as if it were owned at the partnership level. Similarly, if a claimant constructs and incurs the cost to build a structure on land owned by another person (or incorporates capital property into property owned by another as an integral part thereof) without acquiring either a freehold or leasehold interest in the structure, CCA cannot be claimed, and the expenditure is disallowed as an SR&ED capital expenditure. Moreover, even where acquired after December 15, 2024, land is ineligible because it is a non-depreciable asset, and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings (including payments made to an approved university, college, or research organization to the extent the payment may reasonably be considered to have been made to enable the recipient to acquire a building or leasehold interest in a building) are statutorily excluded.

To qualify for 100% capital expenditure inclusion under Paragraph 37(1)(b) and Subsection 127(9), the claimant must intend, at the time of acquisition after December 15, 2024, to either use the depreciable property all or substantially all (ASA)—defined as 90% or more—of its operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value to perform SR&ED in Canada. Generally, operating time means the time the equipment usually runs or functions. Where a claimant's taxation year began before December 16, 2024, and straddles that effective date, the CRA requires the claimant to calculate the SR&ED use (reported on Lines 262 and 263 of Form T661) as a percentage of the total operating time of the equipment specifically for the period after December 15, 2024.

For depreciable equipment acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that is shared between commercial operations and SR&ED and therefore does not meet the 90% ASA threshold over its entire useful life, the post-2024 reforms restore the Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) regime under Subsection 127(9). If the equipment is used primarily (more than 50% of its operating time, excluding GPOEF) for SR&ED in Canada during its first operating period (first-term SUE) and second operating period (second-term SUE), the claimant may claim on Line 504 of Form T661 25% of the capital cost of the equipment in the first period as first-term SUE and the other 25% of the capital cost in the second period as second-term SUE. With respect to leased equipment, lease costs incurred before December 16, 2024 (and after December 31, 2013) do not qualify, whereas lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024, qualify in full if the equipment meets the 90% ASA threshold (excluding GPOEF under the proxy method) or qualify as proportionate overhead on Line 360 under the traditional method if used less than 90% of the time in SR&ED.

Three additional statutory integrity rules in Section 127 govern the boundaries of qualified expenditures across both current and capital outlays. First, under the taxable supplier requirement, a current or contract SR&ED expenditure paid or payable to or for the benefit of a person or partnership that is not a taxable supplier (generally a person resident in Canada or a non-resident carrying on business through a Canadian permanent establishment) is excluded from qualified expenditures unless the claimant made the expenditure for SR&ED that it directly carried out itself. Second, under the unpaid amounts rule in Subsection 127(26), an expenditure incurred in a taxation year that remains unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year is excluded from qualified expenditures for that year; when the expenditure is subsequently paid in a later taxation year, it is deemed incurred in that later year, and in the case of an arm's-length contract expenditure, only 80% of the amount paid in that subsequent year is added to qualified SR&ED expenditures. Third, under the non-arm's length (NAL) adjustment rules in Subsections 127(11.5) and 127(11.6), the amount of an expenditure (other than a prescribed proxy amount) incurred by a taxpayer in a taxation year for a service rendered or property provided by a non-arm's length supplier is deemed to be the actual cost to the NAL supplier of rendering the service or the cost of the property otherwise determined, thereby stripping out intercompany markups. Where a NAL performer transfers qualified expenditures to a payor using Form T1146 (reported on Line 535 and Line 540 of Form T661), capital expenditures and equipment lease costs may only be included if the depreciable property was acquired or the lease cost was incurred after December 15, 2024.
Cloud Computing, AI Infrastructure, and Modern Digital Costs

As Canadian R&D increasingly centres on artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning model training, big data analytics, Internet of Things (IoT) sensor networks, blockchain architectures, and cloud computing, the treatment of remote computing expenses has become a significant focus of CRA compliance reviews. Cloud computing allows an organization to purchase elastic computing power and storage from a third-party provider rather than acquiring physical servers. Under CRA policy, claimants electing the Traditional Method may claim elastic cloud computing costs (such as dedicated GPU clusters and virtual compute instances used exclusively for training experimental algorithms or executing SR&ED test environments) on Line 360 of Form T661 as overhead and other expenditures directly attributable and incremental to the SR&ED project, provided the claimant maintains granular telemetry or billing tags segregating SR&ED compute consumption from commercial production hosting. Conversely, under the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method, general cloud hosting and software subscriptions are treated by CRA auditors as overhead expenses already encompassed within the notional 55% PPA calculation, unless the expenditure qualifies as a post-December 15, 2024 non-GPOEF lease of specific hardware capacity used at least 90% of its operating time in SR&ED in Canada or an eligible data input consumed in the experiment.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Every Canadian province except Prince Edward Island (and the Yukon Territory) offers a distinct corporate income tax credit for R&D conducted within its territorial jurisdiction, creating a layered federal-provincial incentive stack. Under Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" (reported on Line 514 of Form T661). Consequently, provincial credits reduce the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar before the federal 15% or 35% ITC is computed. However, per the CRA's post-2024 update to Line 514 instructions, if provincial or territorial government assistance includes an amount for a capital expenditure that the claimant incurred for property acquired and available for use before December 16, 2024, that capital-related provincial assistance is excluded from Line 514 because the underlying capital asset was ineligible federally.

body.text: Deep-Dive Analysis of Key Provincial Regimes
Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and Capital Expenditure Harmonisation

Ontario operates a three-pronged R&D tax credit system under the Taxation Act, 2007 (S.O. 2007, c. 11), administered jointly with the CRA through the T2 corporate income tax return. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) under Section 96 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (claimed on Schedule 566) provides an 8% refundable tax credit for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016 (reduced from 10% for taxation years ending before June 1, 2016, and prorated for taxation years straddling June 1, 2016) on up to $3,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures performed in Ontario and attributable to a permanent establishment in Ontario, yielding a maximum annual refundable credit of $240,000. Associated corporations must share the $3,000,000 expenditure limit, which is also prorated for short taxation years based on the number of days in the year relative to 365. Notably, Ontario has retained its legacy small-business phase-out thresholds for the OITC: the $3,000,000 expenditure limit is gradually reduced if the corporation's prior-year federal taxable income exceeds $500,000 (and is totally eliminated at $800,000) or if its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $25,000,000 (and is totally eliminated at $50,000,000). Crucially, however, Ontario has updated its definition of OITC qualified expenditures to harmonise with the December 16, 2024 federal capital restoration: an OITC qualified expenditure includes 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024, while continuing to exclude capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013, and before December 16, 2024 (and having included 40% of qualified capital expenditures made before January 1, 2014).

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) under Section 38 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (claimed on Schedule 508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit available to all qualifying corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario on eligible SR&ED expenditures, net of any OITC claimed. As confirmed in the 2025 and 2026 Ontario Fall Economic Statement Tax Expenditure Transparency Reports, the ORDTC automatically incorporates the federal legislative change restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures on property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, with fiscal estimates reported net of any recapture of the tax credit. Third, the Ontario Business Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) under Section 97 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (claimed on Schedule 568) provides a 20% refundable tax credit on up to $20,000,000 of qualified expenditures incurred under an eligible contract with an approved Ontario research institute, such as a university, college of applied arts and technology, or hospital research institute.
Québec: Transition from Legacy Credits to the New Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization

Unlike Ontario and British Columbia, Québec administers its corporate and personal tax system independently through Revenu Québec under the Taxation Act (Québec). Taxpayers claiming Québec R&D incentives must file Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures) alongside specific credit schedules. Revenu Québec's R&D tax architecture is divided by a pivotal effective date—March 25, 2025.

For taxation years (or a partnership's fiscal period, where the taxpayer claims the credit as a member of a partnership) beginning on or before March 25, 2025, claimants utilize Québec's legacy suite of refundable R&D tax credits detailed in Revenu Québec publication IN-109-V (Tax Assistance for Scientific Research and Experimental Development). The primary legacy instrument is the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D), claimed on Form RD-1029.7-V (accompanied by Form RD-1029.7.8-T, Agreement Between Associated Corporations Regarding the Expenditure Limit), which provides a refundable credit on Québec R&D salaries and 50% of arm's-length Québec subcontractor payments at a base rate of 14% and an enhanced rate of up to 30% on the first $3,000,000 of eligible salaries for corporations whose prior-year world-wide assets (including associated corporations) do not exceed $50,000,000 (phasing out linearly to 14% at $75,000,000 of assets), subject to an annual exclusion threshold. The legacy regime also includes the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V), and the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V), none of which may be claimed by a specified member of a partnership or by a trust whose beneficiary is a tax-exempt person, a Crown corporation, or a corporation controlled by a prescribed research entity.

For taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec has eliminated five legacy credits: the tax credit for salaries and wages (R&D), the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or a research consortium, the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research, the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium (subject to transitional rules regarding a partnership's eligible fee balance), and the tax credit for technological adaptation services. Replacing those five eliminated mechanisms is the unified New Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization. Under this reformed regime, a corporation or qualified partnership that carries on a business in Québec, maintains an establishment in Québec, and carries out R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Québec (or has them carried out on its behalf in Québec under contract) may claim a refundable credit on four categories of expenditure: salaries and wages, consideration paid to subcontractors, payments to certain research organizations, and capital expenditures for the acquisition of property. The inclusion of pre-commercialization activities (such as industrial design, regulatory homologation, and pre-production validation) and capital property acquisitions aligns Québec's incentive base with the full innovation commercialization continuum and the federal capital expenditure restoration. The unified credit provides a 20% basic refundable rate—including a 20% rate for a corporation that is a member of a qualified partnership, claimed on lines 440p to 440y using codes 112 and 113 in Guide CO-17.G—and an enhanced 30% refundable rate on up to $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures.
Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) and Formulaic Mechanics

Enacted under Division 7 of Part 6 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act for taxation years ending after December 31, 2020, and administered independently by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) alongside the Ministry of Technology and Innovation, the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) is a refundable corporate tax credit targeting small and medium-sized corporations undertaking R&D in Alberta. As detailed in TRA Information Circular IEG-1R5 (June 2026) and the Guide to Claiming the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant, the IEG utilizes a two-tier incremental formula reported on AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and Form AT4970 (List of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Carried Out in Alberta), with the resulting credit deducted from tax otherwise payable (or refunded) on Line 129 of the Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return (AT1) effective as of the corporation's balance-due day.

Under the statutory formula in Division 7 of Part 6 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, a qualified corporation's IEG is the aggregate of two components: first, 8% of the lesser of the corporation's eligible Alberta R&D expenditures for the taxation year and its maximum expenditure limit; and second, an additional 12% of the amount, if any, by which the lesser of the corporation's eligible expenditures for the taxation year and its maximum expenditure limit exceeds the corporation's base amount (base level of spending), thereby yielding an enhanced 20% combined payment on eligible R&D spending that exceeds the corporation's base spending level. A firm's base level of spending is determined by calculating the corporation's average qualifying R&D spending carried out in Alberta over the previous two taxation years, where only the expenditures in respect of SR&ED carried out in Alberta that were included on Line 559 of federal Form T661 are relevant. If a corporation did not have any eligible Alberta expenditures in the preceding two years, its base amount is nil ($0), allowing its entire eligible expenditure up to the cap to earn the full 20% rate; for example, if a non-associated corporation claiming the IEG had eligible Alberta expenditures of $0 in Year 1 and $20,000 in Year 2, its base amount for Year 3 is $10,000. For associated corporations, the incremental amount to be allocated among qualified corporations in the associated group is determined by the statutory formula.

The maximum annual expenditure limit for the IEG is $4,000,000 (shared among associated corporations and prorated if the taxation year is shorter than 365 days, or 366 days if the taxation year includes February 29). To ensure support targets small and medium-sized companies, the grant phases out incrementally for firms with between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital, and firms with $50,000,000 or more in taxable capital are completely ineligible for the grant. Furthermore, where property whose cost was included in eligible expenditures for an IEG claim is subsequently disposed of or converted to commercial use (including property transferred under a non-arm's length agreement), the Alberta Corporate Tax Act enforces a statutory recapture addition to Alberta tax payable equal to the lesser of (A ÷ B) × C and (A ÷ B) × D × E (or E × [(A ÷ B) × D − F] for transferee dispositions under a subsection 127(13) agreement, where F is any recapture already added for the property), where A represents the IEG for the taxation year in which the property was acquired, B represents the lesser of eligible expenditures and the $4,000,000 maximum expenditure limit for the acquisition year, C is the original cost included in eligible expenditures, D is the proceeds of disposition (or the fair market value on conversion to commercial use or on a non-arm's length disposition), and the remaining ratio E scales the recapture when acquisition-year eligible expenditures exceeded the $4,000,000 maximum expenditure limit.
Integrated Federal-Provincial Stacking Illustration (Post-December 15, 2024 Regime)

Because provincial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, they reduce the federal qualified expenditure pool before the federal ITC is calculated. body.text: As this statutory walkthrough demonstrates, on $1,500,000 of actual cash outlays ($1,000,000 in salaries and $500,000 in capital equipment), the combination of the 55% notional PPA uplift ($550,000), the restored eligibility of capital expenditures on or after December 16, 2024, and the federal-Ontario credit stack generates $867,007 in total tax credits—representing a 57.8% direct tax credit recovery on actual cash outlay, of which $707,778 is immediately cash-refundable via the $543,778 federal refund and $164,000 Ontario OITC refund—before even accounting for the corporate income tax value of deducting the remaining Section 37(1) pool balance.
Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, Pre-Claim Review, and Audit Administration
Division of Institutional Responsibilities

The administration of Canadian R&D incentives involves three distinct federal institutions operating alongside provincial revenue authorities. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) exercises exclusive statutory authority over the administration, technical review, financial audit, and assessment of federal SR&ED claims as well as harmonised provincial R&D credits. Within the CRA, SR&ED claims are evaluated through a bifurcated review process conducted jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA)—a domain scientist or engineer who evaluates whether the claimed work satisfies the "Why" and "How" requirements under Subsection 248(1)—and a Financial Reviewer (FR), a specialized tax auditor who verifies expenditure substantiation, overhead elections, contract arm's-length status, capital asset availability-for-use dates, and government assistance deductions under Sections 37 and 127.

Concurrently, the Department of Finance Canada retains jurisdiction over federal tax policy, legislative drafting of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations, Federal Budget and Fall Economic Statement reforms, and annual Federal Tax Expenditures reporting. Complementing the tax credit system, the National Research Council of Canada – Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) deliver direct, non-repayable innovation grants and clean-technology commercialization support. While a business that receives other government funding such as NRC IRAP grants for R&D may still claim SR&ED tax incentives on the same project, those grants constitute federal "government assistance" that must be deducted on Form T661, reducing the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool for the funded portion while leaving the unfunded salary portion and the 55% PPA on total eligible salaries available to generate SR&ED ITCs.
Mandatory Tax Forms, Pre-Claim Approval, and the 18-Month Statutory Deadline

To perfect a federal SR&ED claim, a taxpayer must submit a prescribed package of forms to the CRA with its income tax return. Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) serves as the cornerstone technical and financial filing, housing both the project-by-project technical narratives (Part 2, requiring rigorous articulation of the scientific or technological uncertainties, hypotheses formulated, systematic experimentation or analysis conducted, and advancements achieved) and the expenditure schedules (Part 3 through Part 5, including Lines 262 and 263 for post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditure operating-time use, Line 360 for traditional method overhead and less-than-90% equipment leases, Line 504 for first-term and second-term Shared-Use Equipment, Line 514 for provincial and territorial government assistance, Lines 535 and 540 for non-arm's length transfers of qualified expenditures, and Line 559 for net qualified SR&ED expenditures). Alongside Form T661, corporate claimants must file Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations)—while individual and unincorporated claimants file Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals))—to compute the 15% or 35% ITC, track the $6,000,000 expenditure limit and its taxable capital or three-year average annual revenue phase-out, calculate the 100% or 40% refundability, and manage the 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward continuity of unused credits. Where applicable, claimants must also file Form T1146 (to transfer qualified expenditures under a non-arm's length SR&ED contract), Form T1174 (to allocate salary or wages of specified employees among associated corporations), and Form T1263 (to report third-party payments for SR&ED).

Under Subsections 37(11) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer's statutory reporting deadline for SR&ED is strictly 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because a corporation's T2 filing-due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, a corporate claimant faces an absolute, non-discretionary 18-month statutory deadline from the end of its taxation year to file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 containing the prescribed information for each project and expenditure. The Minister of National Revenue has no statutory discretion under the taxpayer relief provisions to waive or extend this 18-month SR&ED filing deadline; any expenditure or project omitted when the 18-month window expires is permanently barred from both the Section 37(1) pool and the Section 127 ITC calculation.

To enhance predictability prior to filing, the CRA provides the online SR&ED Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT) alongside a formal Pre-Claim Approval process that enables businesses to determine whether their work is eligible and what information is needed before submitting their claim. Furthermore, Budget 2026 emphasizes accelerated upfront certainty mechanisms—providing binding CRA rulings before capital is committed under a streamlined "1 project · 1 decision · 1 year" framework—to de-risk large-scale R&D and clean-technology capital deployments. Concurrently, on the compliance enforcement side, the CRA engages industry associations to raise awareness of program requirements, applies the elements of its SR&ED Large Claim Strategy to broader claimant populations, and utilizes advanced third-party data analytics to strengthen audit risk assessment.
Judicial Precedents and Tax Court of Canada Jurisprudence

Because the statutory definition of SR&ED in Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act turns on qualitative scientific and engineering concepts, the legal boundaries of the program are continuously refined by the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA). Three foundational judicial authorities govern modern SR&ED audit defence and technical documentation in Canada.
Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998 CanLII 568 (TCC))

Decided by Justice Bowman, Northwest Hydraulic established the classic five-criteria analytical framework derived from Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act that continues to underpin both judicial review and the CRA's modern "Why" and "How" eligibility guidelines. Under Northwest Hydraulic, the Court evaluates first, whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; second, whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty; third, whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses; fourth, whether the process resulted in a technological advancement; and fifth, whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and the results kept, was maintained as the work progressed.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (CanLII)

In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, Justice Sommerfeldt delivered an exhaustive doctrinal synthesis of the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria in the context of mechanical engineering and custom theatrical rigging systems, providing four critical legal clarifications regularly cited by the Tax Court and the CRA. First, at paragraph 17, Justice Sommerfeldt acknowledged that while there is no single definitive statutory definition of the term "routine engineering," it describes techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field and involves applying established engineering principles to resolve design challenges without encountering a fundamental capability gap in underlying engineering knowledge. Second, after reviewing the body of jurisprudence that considered the meaning of the word "hypothesis," Justice Sommerfeldt concluded at paragraph 26 that a hypothesis is "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial"—specifically, a provisional causal proposition formulated prior to testing that posits how manipulating specific variables will resolve the technological uncertainty.

Third, at paragraph 33 of Joel Theatrical Rigging, Justice Sommerfeldt summarized the characteristics that must be present to demonstrate that a scientific method had been adopted, emphasizing that the procedures used must accord with systematic observation, measurement, and experimentation, coupled with the formulation, testing, and iterative modification of hypotheses based on empirical or analytical results rather than ad hoc trial-and-error troubleshooting. Fourth, addressing the fifth criterion at paragraph 46, Justice Sommerfeldt noted that while keeping contemporaneous written records of hypotheses, tests, and results is strongly advisable, "some cases have suggested that a written contemporaneous record of hypotheses tested and results kept may not be absolutely essential" as a rigid legal prerequisite if the taxpayer can otherwise establish through credible, corroborated oral and circumstantial evidence that a systematic investigation occurred.
Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2024 TCC 159 (Court File No. 2023-2126(IT)I)

In the landmark decision Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2024 TCC 159, Justice Bodie of the Tax Court of Canada applied the doctrinal framework of Joel Theatrical Rigging to overturn the CRA's denial of an SR&ED claim in the food-processing and thermal-canning sector, offering vital precedent for small and medium-sized enterprises. In that case, the appellant, Manning Canning Kitchens Inc., sought to develop a commercial process for canning a specialized food product that repeatedly suffered from catastrophic container failures—specifically, "exploding cans"—during thermal processing and stabilization. The Minister of National Revenue disallowed the claim on the basis that the taxpayer had not encountered a true technological uncertainty, had not undertaken a systematic investigation or search in the development of its product, and lacked academic-style contemporaneous records.

Allowing the appeal, Justice Bodie systematically applied Justice Sommerfeldt's holdings in Joel Theatrical Rigging across each element of the statutory test. Citing paragraph 17 of Joel Theatrical Rigging at paragraph 16 of the judgment, Justice Bodie held that the unpredictable chemical and physical interactions causing the exploding cans constituted a genuine technological uncertainty that could not be resolved by routine engineering or standard food-processing procedures. Citing paragraph 26 of Joel Theatrical Rigging at paragraph 18, the Court found that Manning Canning had formulated specific causal statements (hypotheses) to be tested by experiment or trial aimed at isolating the root cause of the exploding cans. Applying paragraph 33 of Joel Theatrical Rigging at paragraphs 19 and 20, Justice Bodie held that the appellant's iterative experimentation accorded with the scientific method and advanced the technological knowledge base, ultimately solving the problem of the exploding cans and enabling Manning Canning to successfully bring a product meeting its objectives to market. Finally, citing paragraph 46 of Joel Theatrical Rigging at paragraph 29, Justice Bodie confirmed that the absence of formal academic laboratory logs was not fatal where the taxpayer's systematic hypotheses, tests, and results were credibly established through the evidentiary record. Manning Canning (2024 TCC 159) confirms that while the Tax Court strictly enforces the substantive requirements of technological uncertainty and hypothesis-driven experimentation, it evaluates documentation and the scientific method pragmatically within the operational reality of an SME.
Strategic Synthesis and Audit Readiness Recommendations

The convergence of the December 16, 2024 federal SR&ED legislative expansion (Annual Statutes 2026, c. 3), Québec's post-March 25, 2025 consolidation into the New Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization, and recent Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2024 TCC 159) creates three high-priority strategic imperatives for Canadian R&D claimants and tax auditors.

First, corporations must overhaul their capital asset availability-for-use tracking and overhead method optimization. With capital expenditures and capital lease costs restored on or after December 16, 2024, claimants must maintain fixed-asset sub-ledgers that document both the exact date depreciable property was acquired and became available for use after December 15, 2024, alongside continuous operating-time logs substantiating whether the asset satisfies the 90% All or Substantially All (ASA) threshold or the >50% Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) first-term and second-term thresholds reported on Lines 262, 263, and 504 of Form T661. Furthermore, claimants leasing specialized R&D equipment used less than 90% in SR&ED after December 15, 2024, or incurring substantial dedicated cloud computing costs for AI and machine learning experimentation, should model whether electing the Traditional Method rather than the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method yields a higher net ITC by unlocking Line 360 overhead claims.

Second, scaling corporations must carefully model the CCPC three-year average annual revenue election versus the prior-year taxable capital phase-out. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, private corporations whose prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000 due to venture capital equity rounds, preferred share issuances, or debt facilities should evaluate electing under Section 3.1.1 of the CRA Investment Tax Credit Policy to compute their $6,000,000 expenditure limit using the ECPC three-year average annual revenue test ($15 million to $75 million corridor) rather than the taxable capital test. Conversely, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations must map their consolidated financial statement group structures to allocate the newly accessible $6,000,000 enhanced 35% refundable expenditure limit across qualifying Canadian R&D subsidiaries.

Third, claimants must align their Part 2 technical narratives on Form T661 with the CRA's "Why/How" framework and the evidentiary standards of Joel Theatrical Rigging and Manning Canning. To withstand joint RTA and Financial Reviewer audit scrutiny without protracted litigation, claimants should structure project narratives around the underlying technological advancement rather than commercial business projects, explicitly demonstrating why standard practice or routine engineering failed (the "Why" requirement) and mapping each chronological iteration of problem definition, hypothesis formulation, systematic testing, and logical conclusion (the "How" requirement) to contemporaneous engineering commits, test logs, and payroll time-tracking records.
